# Tutorial packaging format and validation manifest

## Description

Defines the tutorial packaging format that makes curated tutorials versioned
and testable independently of Dashboard releases. The format is the contract
between authored tutorial content and the Dashboard tutorial gallery: it
specifies how a tutorial is described, how its images are pinned, and how it
is validated against a target release.

## Scope

- Define the tutorial package structure covering:
  - tutorial metadata (identity, core journey covered, intended user level)
  - pinned container image references used by the tutorial
  - a validation manifest describing how the tutorial is tested
- Define versioning rules so a tutorial package evolves and is released
  independently of Dashboard releases
- Ensure the format covers both notebook-form tutorials (launched into a
  workbench) and pipeline-form tutorials (imported as a pipeline)
- Provide a reference tutorial package that exercises every part of the format

## Acceptance Criteria

- A written format specification exists covering metadata, pinned images, and
  the validation manifest for both notebook-form and pipeline-form tutorials
- A reference tutorial package conforming to the specification exists and
  passes format validation
- The validation manifest can express the checks needed to verify a tutorial
  against a target release, including the needs of the six core getting-started
  journeys (first workbench, data prep, first training run, first pipeline,
  first deployment, first RAG app)
- Any content or image-pin change to a package requires a version bump,
  demonstrable on the reference package

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1) — tutorial packaging format (metadata, pinned images, validation
  manifest; versioned and testable independently of Dashboard releases)
- Priority inherited as P0: this epic gates the tutorial gallery and all
  curated tutorial content (HLR-1, HLR-2).

# Dashboard tutorial gallery and one-click launch

## Description

Delivers the tutorial gallery in the Dashboard: a curated, browsable surface
from which a user launches a tutorial into their own project with one click —
opening a workbench preloaded with the tutorial notebook, or importing the
tutorial pipeline into the project.

## Scope

- Gallery surface in the Dashboard listing available tutorial packages,
  presented from the tutorial packaging format's metadata
- One-click launch of a notebook-form tutorial: opening a workbench in the
  user's project with the tutorial notebook loaded, using the package's pinned
  image references
- One-click launch of a pipeline-form tutorial: importing the tutorial
  pipeline into the user's project
- Error handling and empty/degraded states for the gallery (launch failures,
  no tutorials available)

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user can browse the tutorial gallery in the Dashboard and see each
  tutorial's metadata
- Launching a notebook-form tutorial opens a workbench in the user's project
  with the tutorial notebook loaded
- Launching a pipeline-form tutorial imports the pipeline into the user's
  project
- Launch behavior is verified against a tutorial package conforming to the
  tutorial packaging format (the reference package)
- Gallery and launch flows fail gracefully with actionable errors when a
  tutorial package is invalid or a launch fails

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0) — Dashboard tutorial gallery with one-click launch into the
  user's project (workbench with notebook, or pipeline import)

# Curated notebook tutorials for core journeys

## Description

Authors the notebook-form curated tutorials covering the core getting-started
journeys, packaged per the tutorial packaging format and tested against the
current release. This is content authoring: maintained, tested tutorial
notebooks a new user launches from the tutorial gallery into a workbench.

## Scope

- Author notebook tutorials for the core journeys that take notebook form
  (first workbench, data prep, first training run, first deployment, first
  RAG app; the final notebook-form vs pipeline-form allocation per journey is
  coordinated with the pipeline tutorial authoring so all six journeys are
  covered exactly once)
- Package each tutorial per the tutorial packaging format: metadata, pinned
  images, and validation manifest
- Validate each tutorial against the current release via its validation
  manifest
- Keep tutorial content maintained as the platform evolves (this epic
  establishes the initial curated set)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Notebook tutorials covering the notebook-form core journeys exist, one per
  journey, with no journey left uncovered across notebook and pipeline forms
- Each tutorial is packaged per the tutorial packaging format and passes
  format validation
- Each tutorial passes its validation manifest against the current release
- Each tutorial is launchable into a user's project: the workbench opens with
  the tutorial notebook loaded and pinned images resolve
- Tutorial content has been reviewed for technical accuracy and completeness
  of the journey it teaches

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0) — curated tutorials covering the core journeys, tested against
  the current release (notebook-form portion; the pipeline-form portion is
  covered by the pipeline tutorial epic)

The `decompose_complete=true` line must be your **final action** — the pipeline will not launch the review agent until it is set.\n35\t\n36\tIf neither check fires, proceed to Step 1.\n37\t\n38\t## Step 1: Parse Strategy Structure\n39\t\n40\tExtract these sections from the strategy:\n41\t\n42\t- **Affected Components table**: (component name, what changes, owner team)\n43\t- **Impacted Teams table**: (team, components owned, involvement)\n44\t- **High Level Requirements**: with P0/P1/P2 priority\n45\t- **Dependencies table**: (dependency, type, status, impact if blocked)\n46\t- **Acceptance Criteria**: (Given/When/Then with \"measured by\" clauses)\n47\t- **Non-Functional Requirements**\n48\t\n49\tIf any required section is missing, note it as a health warning but proceed with available information.\n50\t\n51\t## Step 1.5: Parse Staff Engineer Input\n52\t\n53\tIf the strategy contains a Staff Engineer Input section that is non-empty (beyond template placeholder text):\n54\t\n55\t- Parse it first — it takes precedence\n56\t- When Staff Engineer Input diverges from AI-generated Technical Approach, use the Staff Engineer Input\n57\t- Log each override for traceability in the decomposition summary\n58\t\n59\t## Step 2: Build Component Graph\n60\t\n61\t**Component name constraint:** Read `.context/rhai-components.txt` for the canonical list of RHAI Jira components. Every epic's `component` value MUST be copied verbatim from this list — never invented, paraphrased, or combined (\"Model Serving Stack\" is invalid; the canonical list has `Serving Runtimes`). Match the strategy's Affected Components to the closest canonical name; when one epic's work spans several strategy components, assign the single most-relevant canonical name and note the span in the decomposition summary. `submit.py` silently strips any component not in the list, leaving the Jira epic component-less. Log any non-obvious mappings in the decomposition summary.\n62\t\n63\tFor each (component, change, owner team) tuple from the Affected Components table:\n64\t\n65\t**Active vs. Passive classification:**\n66\t- **Active component**: Code changes needed → generates epic(s)\n67\t- **Passive component**: No code changes, keep working → validation becomes acceptance criterion on nearest active component's epic\n68\t- **Exception**: If a different team validates the passive component → generate a separate validation Implementation epic owned by that team\n69\t\n70\t**New component detection:**\n71\t- Check `.context/architecture-context/` for component existence\n72\t- Component is \"in platform\" if an architecture context file exists for it\n73\t- Component NOT in architecture context → create:\n74\t  - Implementation epic(s) for provisioning with appropriate `implementation_type`\n75\t  - Investigation epic if dependency availability needs validation\n76\t\n77\t## Step 3: Identify Investigation Epics\n78\t\n79\tFirst, systematically scan the strategy for all unknowns — check the open questions table, risks table, assumptions, pending reviews, and conditional ADRs. Do not rely on the technical approach section alone; open questions are often in tables at the end of the strategy and may contradict or qualify the detailed technical description.\n80\t\n81\tCollect the full list of unknowns before creating any Investigation epics. Then evaluate each independently:\n82\t\n83\t**Decision rule: Does the answer change which downstream epics exist or what they do?**\n84\t\n85\t- **YES** → Investigation epic. Determine which downstream epics depend on the outcome. Add as DAG edges. For bounded outcomes (≤3 possibilities): output conditional decomposition branches.\n86\t- **NO** → Acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic. Implementation proceeds the same way regardless; failure = fix-and-retry.\n87\t\n88\tMultiple independent unknowns can produce multiple Investigation epics, even for the same component and team. The component/team boundary rule applies to Implementations (bundling work for a team), not Investigations (resolving a specific unknown). However, if two qualifying unknowns would be resolved by the same experiment producing the same deliverable, combine them into one Investigation — don't split for the sake of splitting.\n89\t\n90\t## Step 4: Map HLRs to Epics\n91\t\n92\t**Precondition:** This step only runs for strategies that were NOT triaged in Step 0. If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.\n93\t\n94\t- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics\n95\t- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements\n96\t- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables\n97\t- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0\n98\t- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is \"distinct and deferrable\" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. \"select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side\" and \"a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs\" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.\n100\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n101\t\n102\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n103\t\n104\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n105\t\n106\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n107\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n108\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n109\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n110\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.\n111\t   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.\n112\t\n113\t### Investigation Edges\n114\t3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.\n115\t4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.\n116\t\n117\t### Implementation Type Ordering\n118\t5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)\n119\t6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). Doesn't block other repos.\n120\t7. `license-validation` ∥ `repo-onboarding` parallel (independent inputs)\n121\t8. `license-validation` ∥ `konflux-onboarding` parallel (config doesn't depend on specific deps)\n122\t9. `license-validation` → general implementation serial (if licenses fail, deps change, affects approach)\n123\t10. `konflux-onboarding` ∥ general implementation parallel (config independent of code; AC gates first execution). **Add NO blocking edge in either direction.** It is tempting to make the general implementation depend on `konflux-onboarding` (\"the code needs a build pipeline first\") — do not. That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 \"build pipeline green\" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation. This holds for EVERY `konflux-onboarding` × general-implementation pair in the decomposition, whatever the general epic's component or deliverable — a stack-wide assembly, packaging, or evidence epic that consumes the pipeline's outputs is still a general implementation. There is no \"different component\" or \"genuine artifact dependency\" exemption: if the coupling is real, express it as an AC on the consuming epic (\"the signed attestations from the build pipeline are included and validated\"), never as an edge.\n124\t11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.\n125\t\n126\t### Implementation → Implementation Edges\n127\t12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)\n128\t13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a \"pinned image digest available\" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel. The same holds for any build-pipeline output another epic consumes as CONTENT — signed attestations, SBOMs, provenance, scan results: the consuming epic gets an AC (\"the evidence package includes the signed attestations produced by the build pipeline\"), not an edge. Code builds against an API, CRD, or library; it does not build against attestations or digests.\n129\t14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel\n130\t15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)\n131\t\n132\t### External Dependency Edges\n133\t16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)\n134\t17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)\n135\t18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)\n136\t\n137\t### Epic Generation Rules\n138\t19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation\n139\t20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).\n140\t21. External community dependency where team submits PR/RFC and acceptance gates downstream → generate upstream Implementation epic, evaluate tiered delivery. If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.\n141\t22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation\n142\t\n143\t### Acceptance Criteria Rules\n144\t23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n145\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n146\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n147\t\n148\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n149\t\n150\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n151\t\n152\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n153\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n154\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n155\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n156\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n157\t\n158\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n159\t\n160\tFor each epic, determine:\n161\t\n162\t### Type (mandatory)\n163\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n164\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n165\t\n166\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n167\t\n168\t| Label | When to apply |\n169\t|-------|--------------|\n170\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n171\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n172\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n173\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n174\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n175\t\n176\t### AI Implementability Signals\n177\t\n178\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n179\t\n180\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n181\t\n182\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |\n195\t\n196\t**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state (\"shipped as Tech Preview\", \"generally available\"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word \"claim\". A strategy premise that drives the decomposition (e.g. a maturity gap motivating a hardening program) is an architecture claim. Check `.context/architecture-context/` for the epic's components: score +1 when a context file corroborates the premise or grounds the epic's scope, and cite that file in the rationale; score -1 when the strategy asserts something the context contradicts; score 0 only when no context file covers any component the epic touches. \"The strategy makes no specific architecture claims\" is not a valid 0 rationale when context files exist for the components in scope.\n197\t\n198\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n199\t\n200\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n201\t\n202\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n203\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n204\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n205\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n206\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n207\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n208\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n209\t\n210\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n211\t\n212\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n213\t\n214\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n215\t\n216\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n217\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n218\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n219\t\n220\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n221\t\n222\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n223\t\n224\t| Situation | Handling |\n225\t|-----------|---------|\n226\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n227\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n228\t\n229\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n230\t\n231\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n232\t\n233\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n234\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n235\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n236\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n237\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n238\t\n239\tEvery AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable — something the epic's engineering work produces or verifies. Externally-controlled preconditions are not ACs, in either form: schedule constraints (turnaround you do not control — accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) or availability preconditions (procurement, dedicated hardware or node allocation, partner-lab access, environment provisioning) — anything granted by parties outside the strategy belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — \"the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged\" is a valid AC; \"lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed\" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC; \"dedicated hardware nodes are available to the campaign\" is an availability precondition misfiled as an AC — the epic's work may include *securing* access, but the access being granted is not a condition the epic's deliverable produces, so it stays in Risks/Notes while the AC sits on the deliverable itself (e.g. the campaign's validated report).\n240\t\n241\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n242\t\n243\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n244\t\n245\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n246\t\n247\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n248\t\n249\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n250\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n251\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n252\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n253\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n254\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n255\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n256\t\n257\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n258\t\n259\t```bash\n260\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n261\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n262\t```\n263\t\n264\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n265\t\n266\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n267\t\n268\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n269\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n270\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n271\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n272\tfor the implementing team.\n273\t\n274\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n275\t\n276\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n277\t\n278\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n279\t\n280\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n281\t   - **Title** (one line)\n282\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n283\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n284\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n285\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n286\t   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).\n287\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n288\t\n289\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability.
